(CNN) -- Tom Cruise expounds on his beliefs in Scientology in a 2004 video that made its way onto the Internet this week. Tom Cruise appears with his wife, Katie Holmes, at a movie premiere earlier this month. "I think it's a privilege to call yourself a Scientologist, and it's something you have to earn," Cruise says at the beginning of the video. Cruise says he's "driven ... by the opportunity to really help, for the first time, change people's lives. I'm absolutely, uncompromisingly dedicated to that." The video was shown at a 2004 Scientology ceremony honoring Cruise for his humanitarian work. Church of Scientology officials said it can be viewed at any of its churches, but it created a stir this week when what the church calls a pirated and edited version appeared on YouTube. The video has since been taken off YouTube, but an interview portion remained available on the celebrity Web site gawker.com on Thursday.  Watch snippets of Cruise video » . "The Cruise Indoctrination Video Scientology Tried To Suppress" is the title of gawker.com's presentation. "You have to watch this video," the site says. "It shows Tom Cruise, with all the wide-eyed fervor that he brings to the promotion of a movie, making the argument for Scientology," which it calls "the bizarre 20th-century religion.  Watch "Showbiz Tonight" discussion of Cruise video » . Cruise talks over a repetitive guitar-riff soundtrack, and appears to be answering questions, though an interviewer is not seen or heard. A second part of the video, made available to CNN by the publisher of a new unauthorized biography of Cruise, shows Cruise accepting Scientology's Freedom Medal of Valor award and exchanging military-like salutes with Scientology chairman David Miscavige to audience applause. The publisher denies leaking other parts of the video to the Web. In the video by the publisher, Cruise also salutes a portrait of L. Ron Hubbard, cited on the church's Web site as the founder of "the only major religion founded in the 20th century." Hubbard's biography cites his accomplishments as everything from mariner and horticulturalist to author and humanitarian. In the video, Cruise puts emphasis on the latter role. A Scientologist "has the ability to create new realities and improve conditions," Cruise says. On its Web site, the Church of Scientology highlights its humanitarian work, from anti-drug campaigns in places from Minnesota to Taiwan to teacher training in India. The Web site defines Scientology as "the study of truth." Cruise embraces that in the video. "If you're a Scientologist, ... you see things the way they are," Cruise says. He also says he finds peace in the religion. "The more you know as a Scientologist, you don't become overwhelmed by it," according to Cruise. The unauthorized biography of Cruise is by author Andrew Morton. A Cruise spokesperson and the Church of Scientology have disputed the book, saying Morton did not seek their comment. "Accuracy and truth were not on Morton's agenda," according to a church statement. Morton denies that and says Cruise, who he calls "a towering figure on the international scene," and his faith are worthy of scrutiny. "Tom Cruise has done remarkable work for his faith over the past few years," Morton said. "If it wasn't for him the Church of Scientology would be a shadow of what it is today." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Brad Lendon, David Mattingly and Don Lemon contributed to this report.

CNN also obtained another portion of the recording from the publisher of a new unauthorized biography of Cruise. That segment shows Cruise receiving Scientology’s Freedom Medal of Valor and exchanging military-style salutes with David Miscavige, the church’s chairman, while the audience applauds. The publisher has denied being responsible for leaking other sections of the video online.

In the publisher-provided footage, Cruise is also shown saluting a portrait of L. Cruise says in the recording that a Scientologist “has the ability to create new realities and improve conditions.” The Church of Scientology’s website emphasizes its humanitarian programs, including anti-drug initiatives in locations ranging from Minnesota to Taiwan and teacher-training efforts in India. Morton rejects that criticism. He argues that Cruise, whom he describes as a major international figure, and Cruise’s religion are legitimate subjects for examination. ## Tom Cruise’s Scientology Video Resurfaces Online Amid Controversy and Renewed Scrutiny Around Andrew Morton Biography

Tom Cruise’s association with the Church of Scientology has long been one of Hollywood’s most scrutinized celebrity-religion relationships, but few moments intensified public attention as dramatically as the online circulation of a Scientology promotional video featuring the actor. The clip, originally intended for internal Church use, became a major internet controversy after it appeared on news and gossip sites, triggering legal threats, debate over censorship, and renewed interest in claims made in Andrew Morton’s unauthorized biography of Cruise.

The video showed Cruise speaking passionately about Scientology, describing his commitment to the religion and its mission in terms that quickly became the subject of intense public discussion. In the clip, Cruise discussed Scientologists as people uniquely equipped to help in crises and referred to the role of Scientology in his life and worldview. His emphatic delivery, combined with dramatic music and Church-produced framing, made the video instantly viral once it escaped its intended audience.

For Cruise, already one of the most famous actors in the world, the video became another flashpoint in a period when his public image was under unusual pressure. It followed years of headlines about his outspoken advocacy for Scientology, his criticism of psychiatry and prescription medication, and his highly publicized relationship with Katie Holmes. Although Cruise remained a dominant box-office figure, the video fueled renewed debate about the extent to which his religious beliefs influenced his public persona and career.

### The Online Leak and Rapid Spread

The Scientology video began circulating widely online after it was posted by several websites, most notably Gawker, which published the footage in January 2008. The Church of Scientology objected to its publication, asserting that the video was copyrighted material and not meant for public distribution.

What followed was a classic early-internet clash between a powerful institution seeking to control proprietary material and web publishers arguing that the footage was newsworthy. Gawker refused to remove the video, framing the publication as a matter of public interest because of Cruise’s celebrity status and his prominent role as a public advocate for Scientology.

The dispute quickly expanded beyond entertainment gossip. It became a debate over copyright, press freedom, and the so-called “Streisand effect,” in which efforts to suppress material online can make it exponentially more visible. As legal pressure mounted, copies of the video appeared across multiple platforms, blogs, and file-sharing sites, making containment nearly impossible.

### Anonymous and “Project Chanology”

The controversy also became closely tied to the rise of Anonymous as an activist force. After the Church attempted to remove the video from the internet, members of online communities associated with Anonymous launched what became known as “Project Chanology,” a campaign criticizing Scientology and protesting what participants described as censorship.

Anonymous released videos, organized demonstrations, and staged protests outside Scientology centers around the world. Many demonstrators wore Guy Fawkes masks, an image that later became strongly associated with internet-driven protest movements. While Anonymous had existed previously as a loose online collective, the Cruise video controversy was one of the events that helped transform it into a more visible activist network.

The Church of Scientology has long disputed many criticisms made by opponents and has characterized some campaigns against it as harassment or religious bigotry. But the public conflict over the Cruise video gave critics a high-profile rallying point and placed Scientology under a level of internet scrutiny it had rarely experienced before.

### Andrew Morton’s Unauthorized Biography

The timing of the video’s circulation was especially significant because it overlapped with renewed attention on Andrew Morton’s unauthorized biography, *Tom Cruise: An Unauthorized Biography*, published in 2008. Morton, best known for his explosive biography of Princess Diana, turned his focus to Cruise’s life, career, marriages, and involvement with Scientology.

The book made a range of claims about Cruise’s relationship with the Church and its influence on his personal and professional world. Because the biography was unauthorized, Cruise did not participate, and many of its assertions were disputed by Cruise’s representatives and the Church of Scientology. The Church strongly criticized the book, reportedly describing it as inaccurate and sensationalized.

Morton’s biography arrived at a moment when public curiosity about Cruise and Scientology was already intense. The leaked video gave the book additional relevance in entertainment media because both centered on the same larger question: how closely Cruise’s public identity was tied to Scientology, and how much that connection shaped perceptions of him.

### Cruise, Scientology, and Public Image

By the late 2000s, Cruise’s public image had gone through several dramatic phases. For much of the 1980s and 1990s, he was defined primarily by his status as a charismatic movie star, with roles in *Top Gun*, *Rain Man*, *A Few Good Men*, *Jerry Maguire*, and *Mission: Impossible*. His private life was covered heavily, but his religious affiliation was not always central to mainstream coverage.

That changed in the 2000s. Cruise became more publicly vocal about Scientology, and several high-profile media appearances drew scrutiny. His 2005 interview with Matt Lauer, in which he criticized psychiatry and questioned actress Brooke Shields’s use of antidepressants for postpartum depression, became one of the defining celebrity controversies of the decade. His energetic appearance on *The Oprah Winfrey Show* that same year also became a pop culture moment, widely replayed and parodied.

Against that backdrop, the Scientology video seemed to confirm for many viewers that Cruise’s religious commitment was not merely private but central to his public identity. Supporters saw it as evidence of conviction and dedication; critics viewed it as unsettling or excessive. Either way, the video became one of the most discussed celebrity clips of its era.

### The Legal and Ethical Debate

The publication of the video raised difficult questions about the boundaries of celebrity journalism. Was an internal religious video fair game because it featured one of the world’s most famous actors? Or was its release an invasion of institutional privacy and copyright?

Gawker and other defenders of publication argued that the video was newsworthy because Cruise was not simply a private member of the Church but one of Scientology’s most recognizable public figures. They also argued that the Church’s efforts to suppress the video made the story more significant.

The Church maintained that the footage was protected material and that unauthorized distribution violated its rights. Its response reflected a broader history of aggressively challenging media portrayals it considers false, defamatory, or improperly obtained.

The controversy became an important case study in how digital media had changed celebrity reporting. In an earlier era, a disputed video might have been contained through legal action or industry pressure. By 2008, however, once a clip entered the online ecosystem, takedown demands often accelerated its spread.

### Morton’s Book and the Media Storm

Morton’s biography fed directly into the media storm because it provided a larger narrative around Cruise’s life and Scientology involvement. Entertainment outlets, tabloids, and television programs connected the video to Morton’s book, treating both as part of a broader reconsideration of Cruise’s public image.

The book reportedly examined Cruise’s marriages to Mimi Rogers, Nicole Kidman, and Katie Holmes, as well as his rise within Hollywood and his relationship with Scientology leaders. Many of the most provocative claims were denied or challenged, and readers were left to navigate competing accounts from Morton, anonymous sources, Cruise’s camp, and the Church.

What made the biography particularly controversial was not simply that it discussed Scientology, but that it suggested the Church played a major role in Cruise’s personal and professional life. Cruise’s representatives and Scientology officials rejected what they characterized as distortions, while Morton defended his reporting.

### Lasting Impact

Although the immediate frenzy eventually faded, the Scientology video remains a landmark moment in celebrity internet culture. It demonstrated how quickly private or semi-private material could become global entertainment news, how legal efforts to remove content could backfire, and how online communities could turn a celebrity controversy into a broader activist campaign.

For Tom Cruise, the episode became part of a complicated public narrative. Over time, his box-office reputation rebounded strongly, particularly through the continuing success of the *Mission: Impossible* franchise and later blockbuster triumphs such as *Top Gun: Maverick*. Cruise’s image shifted again toward that of a highly disciplined action star and defender of theatrical moviegoing.

Still, the video’s circulation remains one of the most memorable controversies of his career. Paired with Andrew Morton’s unauthorized biography, it marked a moment when Cruise’s private beliefs, public advocacy, and superstar image collided in full view of the internet. The result was not just a celebrity scandal, but a turning point in how Hollywood, religion, copyright, and digital culture intersected in the modern media age.
